lead: Today the Church remembers St Julius, Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352. St Paul tells us what the Easter peace is: “since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,” and even suffering becomes a road to a hope that does not disappoint. In Matthew, Jesus says that whoever welcomes his messengers welcomes him, and that not even a cup of cold water given to a little one will be forgotten. St Julius lived both readings: he stood firm in the faith of Nicaea and welcomed St Athanasius when he was driven from his see.

set: In Romans 1–4 Paul has shown that all, Jews and Gentiles alike, need the grace of God, and that God makes people righteous through faith in Christ, as he reckoned Abraham righteous through faith (4:3). Chapter 4 ends with an Easter confession: Jesus “was handed over to death for our trespasses and was raised for our justification” (4:25). Chapter 5 begins with what follows from this.
str: vv. 1–2: justified by faith, we have peace with God, access to grace and the hope of glory.
vv. 3–4: we boast even in sufferings: suffering, endurance, character, hope.
v. 5: hope does not disappoint, for God's love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit.
kw: Made righteous, set right with God. In the Catholic faith this is not only a verdict: God forgives sin and truly renews the person within (CCC 1989).
Literally the quality of something that has been tested and proved, like metal that has passed through the fire.
The tense tells of something done that goes on: the love was poured and is still flowing. The image recalls God's promise, “I will pour out my spirit on all flesh” (Joel 2:28).
vv: Therefore, since we are justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,

A note on the text. Many ancient manuscripts read “let us have peace” instead of “we have peace”; in Greek the two differ by a single letter. Most editors prefer “we have”, as the NRSV does, while the Malayalam POC follows the other reading. Both are true: peace is a gift given, and a gift to be lived.
through whom we have obtained access to this grace in which we stand;
Grace is not a passing visit but ground to stand on.
and hope does not disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit that has been given to us.
Hope does not put us to shame, for it rests not on our own strength but on God's love already given. “God's love” here is first God's love for us, and it becomes our love for him.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 5 when it teaches that God is Love and that love is his first gift, poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit (CCC 733). It calls justification the most excellent work of God's love (CCC 1994). St Augustine returned to this verse again and again, above all in his work On the Spirit and the Letter, where it is the key to his teaching that grace is the love of God given to us (in substance).

set: These verses close the missionary discourse of Matthew 10, in which Jesus sends the Twelve to proclaim that the Kingdom of heaven has come near (10:7). He has warned them of rejection and persecution (10:16–39). He ends with the other side: the welcome they will receive, and its reward.

Jewish teaching of the time knew the principle that a person's envoy is like the person himself (Mishnah, Berakhot 5:5). Jesus takes it further: the one who receives his messenger receives him, and through him the Father.
str: v. 40: to welcome you is to welcome me and the one who sent me.
v. 41: to welcome a prophet or a righteous person brings their reward.
v. 42: even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones will not lose its reward.
kw: To receive a guest into one's house. For travelling missionaries, welcome meant a roof, a meal and a hearing.
In Matthew these are the disciples themselves, ordinary believers without rank (18:6, 10, 14). The least disciple carries the Lord's honour.
The smallest gift a poor home could offer. In a hot land, cool water from a deep well was itself a kindness.
vv: Whoever welcomes you welcomes me, and whoever welcomes me welcomes the one who sent me.
Hospitality becomes a meeting with God. The door opened to the messenger is opened to the Father.
and whoever gives even a cup of cold water to one of these little ones in the name of a disciple
“In the name of a disciple” means because he is a disciple, for Christ's sake. The gift is small, but the reason gives it weight.
truly I tell you, none of these will lose their reward.
The reward is not a wage earned but the generosity of God, who notices what everyone else forgets.
ch: The Catechism teaches that our merit before God comes from his grace, which goes before us and goes with us, so that every reward is first his gift (CCC 2008–2011). St Julius is a living commentary on verse 40. When St Athanasius, Bishop of Alexandria, was driven from his see for holding to the faith of Nicaea, Julius received him at Rome, and a council held there under Julius declared him innocent. In welcoming the persecuted bishop, the Bishop of Rome welcomed Christ.

qa: Paul says that we are justified by faith. Does that make good works unimportant?

No. The Catholic Church teaches that we are justified by grace, received through faith and Baptism, and that this grace makes us truly righteous and bears fruit in works of love. Good works done in grace are pleasing to God and merit reward, but only because God's grace first made them possible (CCC 2008, 2010). Today's Gospel shows it: even a cup of cold water given for Christ's sake is not forgotten.
rite: St Julius I was Bishop of Rome from 337 to 352, in the years of the great struggle over the faith of Nicaea. His letter to the bishops gathered at Antioch, which St Athanasius preserved, pleads for fairness and for the communion of the Churches. The Syro-Malankara Catholic Church, Antiochene in heritage and in full communion with the successor of Peter, can see in him a Pope who cared for the faith and the bishops of the East.
study: Paul says that suffering can produce endurance, character and hope. What present difficulty can I offer to God so that it becomes a road to hope?
Whom can I welcome this week in Christ's name, even with a small kindness like a cup of cold water?
